This paper presents a broad empirical study of task-specific knowledge distillation for natural language generation under a practically motivated setup: medium-resource labeled data, abundant unlabeled task-specific inputs, off-the-shelf pretrained models, and a strong emphasis on inference efficiency. The central technical message is that pseudo-target training can be pushed much further than the standard “single beam-generated sequence-level KD” recipe. The paper studies multiple pseudo-targets, sampled rather than beam-generated pseudo-targets, pseudo-targets for unlabeled inputs, and a new Joint-Teaching method that mixes teacher- and student-generated prefixes while applying token-level KD. The experiments span several English-to-English NLG tasks and compare architectural choices, pruning strategies, and KD objectives.

Overall, I found the paper interesting, practically relevant, and stronger as a systematic empirical study than as a sharply isolated methodological contribution. Its main value lies in assembling a coherent distillation recipe for conditional NLG and validating it across multiple tasks and student-teacher pairs. The paper also raises a useful perspective on exposure bias in the KD setting, and the proposed Joint-Teaching idea is intuitive and potentially impactful. At the same time, several aspects of the experimental methodology and presentation weaken the strength of the conclusions. In particular, the sequential stage-wise model selection protocol, the aggregation of results via “fraction of gap closed,” limited statistical treatment, and some fairness issues in architecture comparisons make it harder to assess how robust and general the findings really are.

The strongest aspect of the paper is its practical orientation. Many KD papers in NLP either focus on encoder-only models, high-resource settings, or a single task. Here, the authors explicitly target a realistic deployment scenario for conditional generation, where unlabeled inputs are plentiful and inference cost matters more than one-time training cost. This framing is compelling and likely useful to practitioners. I also appreciate that the paper reports latency and throughput in addition to FLOPs and parameter counts; this is often missing in compression papers and is genuinely valuable.

The empirical findings are also mostly sensible and useful. The observation that encoder-decoder models outperform decoder-only models for task-specific conditional NLG is plausible and supported by the reported averages, though I will return to caveats about fairness. The decoder-pruning result is also practically meaningful: for autoregressive generation, decoder depth affects latency much more directly than encoder depth, so the recommendation to prune the decoder first is actionable. The pseudo-target results are perhaps the most important contribution: the paper shows consistent gains from adding unlabeled inputs, using multiple pseudo-targets, and preferring sampling over beam search for PT generation. These are concrete takeaways that could influence future KD pipelines.

I also think the Joint-Teaching idea is promising. Conditioning KD on student-generated prefixes while using the teacher as a corrective oracle is a natural way to address exposure bias in distillation. The intuition is sound, and the empirical gains over teacher-only or student-only PT training are encouraging. Even if the method is relatively simple, it is a meaningful extension of sequence-level KD practice.

That said, I have several concerns about the rigor of the study and the strength of some claims.

My main methodological concern is the stage-wise experimental design. The paper makes a sequence of decisions, selecting one option at each stage based on average development performance and then carrying only that choice forward. This is understandable from a compute perspective, but it introduces path dependence and can obscure interactions between factors. For example, the best KD objective without PTs need not remain best once unlabeled PTs or Joint-Teaching are introduced. Likewise, the best PT decoding strategy may depend on whether the objective is logits KD alone or logits+sequence-level KD, or on the student architecture. Because the paper does not evaluate a factorial combination of the main choices, the final “recipe” should be interpreted more cautiously than the paper sometimes suggests. It is a reasonable heuristic pipeline, but not necessarily evidence that each selected component is globally optimal in combination with the others.

Relatedly, the paper often phrases conclusions strongly (“use Logits KD,” “sampling is better than beam search,” “Joint-Teaching improves the student”), but the evidence is mostly based on averages over a modest number of setups and without uncertainty estimates. Since many of the reported differences are not huge, confidence intervals or significance tests would help substantially. At minimum, the paper should report variance across random seeds for key comparisons. As written, it is difficult to know whether some of the stage-to-stage gains are robust or partly due to noise from fine-tuning and decoding.

A second concern is the use of the “fraction of student-teacher gap closed” as the primary summary statistic. This metric is intuitive, but it can be unstable and potentially misleading when teacher-student gaps differ substantially across tasks, metrics, or model pairs. It also makes cross-metric aggregation awkward, especially when mixing BLEU, ROUGE, BERTScore, and perplexity, which have different scales and sensitivities. In some cases, a small absolute improvement can look large if the original gap is small. The paper does provide some absolute numbers in Table 4, which is helpful, but the main conclusions rely heavily on the normalized gap metric. I would strongly prefer more direct reporting of absolute task metrics for all major ablations in the main paper, even if only for representative tasks or averaged in a more transparent way.

A third issue is fairness and interpretation in the architecture comparison between encoder-decoder and decoder-only models. The paper argues that ED models outperform DO models for task-specific NLG while having comparable practical efficiency. This may well be true in the studied setup, but the comparison is not entirely clean. The models differ not only in architecture but also in pretraining objectives, tokenizers, scaling histories, and likely fine-tuning suitability. Comparing T5/BART against GPT-2/OPT is informative from a practitioner standpoint, but it does not isolate architecture as the causal factor. The paper should soften the claim accordingly and frame it as a comparison of available model families under task-specific fine-tuning, rather than a definitive architectural conclusion.

The pruning study is useful but also somewhat narrow. Only one pruning scheme is considered, only for BART-6:6, and the pruning strategy is very coarse (dropping layers while keeping first and last). This is enough to support a practical observation, but not enough to justify a broad rule beyond the studied setup. It would help if the paper more clearly distinguished between “in our experiments, decoder pruning was preferable” and a general recommendation.

On the pseudo-target side, I think the paper’s central empirical message is strong, but the mechanistic explanation around exposure bias is less convincing than the authors suggest. The paper claims this is the first work to discuss exposure bias in KD and uses that perspective to motivate PT augmentation and Joint-Teaching. The intuition is reasonable, but the evidence is limited. Figure 2 is only a single setup analysis, and the observed gains from PT diversity could also be explained by standard data augmentation, label smoothing-like effects, or better coverage of output modes, without invoking exposure bias specifically. I would encourage the authors to present exposure bias as one plausible interpretation rather than a demonstrated causal explanation. More targeted experiments would be needed to substantiate the claim, for example evaluating robustness under forced prefix perturbations, measuring error accumulation directly, or comparing against scheduled sampling-style baselines adapted to KD.

I also found the GPT-4 “extreme setup” section somewhat underdeveloped relative to the rest of the paper. It is interesting that some conclusions transfer and others do not, but the experiments are limited to two datasets and a small number of examples, and the discussion attributes mixed results to tokenizer mismatch without much evidence. This section is better viewed as an exploratory appendix-level extension than a core contribution. If kept prominent, it should be framed more cautiously.

There are also some presentation issues. The paper is generally understandable, but the writing contains many grammatical errors and typos throughout, sometimes enough to distract from the content. Examples include repeated subject-verb agreement issues, misspellings, and awkward phrasing. The tables are information-rich, but some are hard to parse, especially because the main text relies on shorthand stage labels and aggregated percentages. The paper would benefit from a cleaner exposition of exactly what data each method trains on at each stage, how many PTs are used, and what decoding hyperparameters are selected. Some of this may be in the appendix, but the main paper should still make the core recipe easy to reconstruct.

A few additional questions and concerns came to mind while reading:

First, how sensitive are the conclusions to the 1:4 labeled/unlabeled ratio? Since unlabeled PTs are a major part of the contribution, it would be useful to know whether gains saturate quickly or continue growing with more unlabeled data. A scaling curve would strengthen the practical relevance.

Second, how many PTs per example are used in the “multiple PT” setting, and how does performance trade off against PT generation cost? Since the paper explicitly emphasizes practical deployment, a cost-performance curve would be very valuable.

Third, are the gains from sampling due to diversity per se, or simply due to generating more total sequences? A controlled comparison matching the number of PTs and perhaps diversity statistics would help isolate this.

Fourth, for Joint-Teaching, why is the 50% teacher/student PT mixing ratio fixed? Is this tuned? Does a curriculum, such as increasing student-generated PT usage over time, work better? Since the method is motivated by exposure bias, scheduling seems especially relevant.

Fifth, the paper mentions end-to-end fine-tuning on gold labels after KD. It would help to know how much of the final gain comes from this post-distillation step and whether all methods benefit equally from it.

Sixth, the evaluation relies entirely on automatic metrics except for a limited ART human evaluation in the appendix. Given that some tasks, especially abductive reasoning and style transfer, are not perfectly captured by BLEU/ROUGE/BERTScore, broader human evaluation would strengthen the claims.

Despite these concerns, I think the paper has real merit. The empirical study is broad, the practical framing is strong, and the pseudo-target findings are useful. My overall assessment is positive but not unreservedly so: I see this as a valuable applied/systematic study whose conclusions should be stated more carefully and whose experimental rigor could be improved.

To strengthen the paper, I would recommend the following revisions. Report variance across multiple seeds for the main ablations, at least for the key stage comparisons and final methods. Include more absolute metric tables in the main paper rather than relying primarily on normalized gap-closure percentages. Soften causal claims about architecture and exposure bias unless supported by more targeted experiments. Clarify the exact PT generation settings and training recipe in the main text. If possible, add one or two interaction experiments to test whether the stage-wise choices remain optimal when combined, especially for Logits KD versus Noisy KD under the final PT regime, and for beam versus sampling under matched PT counts and costs. A small ablation on the amount of unlabeled data and the number of PTs per example would also substantially improve the paper.

In summary, this is a useful and practically relevant paper with a solid empirical contribution, especially regarding pseudo-target augmentation for NLG distillation. Its main weaknesses are methodological: the sequential selection protocol, limited statistical evidence, and somewhat overstated interpretations. With more careful framing and stronger ablation rigor, this could become a strong reference for task-specific KD in conditional generation. As it stands, I view it as a worthwhile contribution, particularly for practitioners, though not yet as definitive as some of its claims imply.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper presents a broad empirical study of task-specific knowledge distillation for natural language generation under a medium-resource setting with additional unlabeled data. It compares encoder-decoder vs. decoder-only architectures, pruning strategies, several KD objectives, and a family of pseudo-target (PT) augmentation methods. The main proposed method is Joint-Teaching, which applies word-level KD on PTs generated by both teacher and student to address exposure bias. Across four English-to-English NLG tasks and two teacher-student pairs, the paper reports that encoder-decoder models are preferable for task-specific NLG, decoder pruning is better than encoder pruning, unlabeled-data PTs help substantially, multiple sampled PTs outperform single beam PTs, and Joint-Teaching yields the best average distilled performance. An additional exploratory section studies distillation from GPT-4 in a no-labeled-data setup.
strengths: The paper tackles a practically important problem: compressing NLG systems for deployment while leveraging unlabeled task-specific data, which is underexplored relative to NLU distillation.
The study is unusually broad, covering architecture choice, pruning, KD objectives, PT generation strategies, unlabeled data usage, and a new Joint-Teaching variant.
The empirical setup spans multiple tasks rather than a single benchmark, which improves the practical relevance of the conclusions.
The paper reports both quality metrics and deployment-oriented efficiency metrics such as latency and throughput, which is valuable for systems-oriented evaluation.
The pseudo-target analysis is useful and the finding that multiple sampled PTs outperform the standard single beam PT is interesting and potentially impactful for practitioners.
The final distilled models appear to recover a large fraction of teacher performance while achieving substantial inference speedups.
The paper is generally candid about limitations, especially around training cost and the constrained GPT-4 experiments.
weaknesses: The work is framed as a systematic study, but the sequential stage-wise model selection procedure introduces strong path dependence; conclusions at later stages depend on earlier choices and may not hold under alternative combinations.

Many central claims are supported only empirically and averaged over heterogeneous tasks/models, with limited statistical rigor; there are no significance tests or uncertainty estimates for the reported gains.

The proposed exposure-bias motivation is suggestive rather than convincingly established. The causal link between PT augmentation / Joint-Teaching and exposure-bias reduction is not directly measured.
The evaluation aggregates disparate metrics into a single 'fraction of gap closed' score, which can be hard to interpret and may obscure absolute performance differences or metric-specific failures.

The architecture comparison between encoder-decoder and decoder-only models is not fully controlled for pretraining data, objective, tokenizer, and adaptation recipe, so the conclusion that ED is better may partly reflect confounds beyond architecture.
The pruning study is narrow: only one pruning heuristic and one BART base model are considered, limiting the generality of the decoder-pruning conclusion.
The GPT-4 extreme setup is too limited to strongly support transferability of the main conclusions; the authors themselves report mixed results.
Some datasets and setup choices are custom or modified (e.g., Shake7, labeled/unlabeled ratios), which may reduce reproducibility and external validity unless all details are fully released.
methodological_flaws: The sequential experimental design is a methodological weakness for a paper claiming systematic conclusions. Because each stage fixes the best option from the previous stage based on dev performance, interactions between factors are not explored; this can lead to suboptimal or misleading conclusions if, for example, the best PT strategy depends on the KD objective or student architecture.

The main summary statistic, (KD-S)/(T-S), is problematic when teacher-student gaps differ greatly across tasks/metrics and can be unstable or misleading when the denominator is small. It also allows values above 100%, which the paper reports, making cross-setting comparisons less principled.

The claim that this is the 'first exposure bias perspective for KD' is not sufficiently substantiated, and the evidence provided (Figure 2) is limited to a single setup. This is not a proof of the proposed mechanism, only a narrow empirical observation.

The teacher-better-than-student assumption for conditioning on student prefixes is only partially validated in one dataset/model setting. Joint-Teaching is then generalized to all tasks without demonstrating that the assumption consistently holds.

The architecture comparison is not a clean scientific comparison of ED vs DO because the compared model families differ in many dimensions besides architecture (pretraining corpus, objective, scale, tokenizer, optimization history). Therefore the causal conclusion about architecture superiority is overstated.
The paper does not report variance across random seeds or confidence intervals. Given the moderate dataset sizes and many compared methods, some reported improvements may be within run-to-run noise.

The omission of training-time computational cost is a notable empirical validity issue because several proposed methods rely on generating many PTs and repeated teacher/student decoding. Since the paper advocates these methods as practical, excluding training cost weakens the practical validity of the conclusions.

The GPT-4 section introduces additional confounds (different tokenizer, zero-shot prompting, inaccessible logits in standard APIs, tiny experimental scope), so it does not provide strong evidence that the main recipe transfers to large proprietary teachers.
